title: The Potential Bench
summary: Map potential around charges, find where it is zero, add potentials at a centre and read a dipole’s potential.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 2.3, Potential due to a point charge
concepts: Potential of a point charge, V = kq/r
Work to bring a charge from infinity
Potential of a system of charges
Points where the potential is zero
learningOutcome: The student can find the potential of one charge or several, the work to bring a charge in from infinity, where the potential is zero, and the potential of a dipole.

levels.title: Probe the potential
levels.adds: Baseline: V = kq/r is a scalar with the sign of the charge, and bringing a charge in from infinity takes work qV.
hints: V = kq/r, with q in coulombs and r in metres. It takes the sign of q.
The potential at infinity is zero. Work to bring q₀ in from infinity is W = q₀V.
A negative potential gives negative work: the field helps.

levels.title: Add them up
levels.adds: New idea: potentials add as plain numbers, so equal charges never cancel even where the field is zero (Ex 2.2).
hints: Potential is a scalar: add kq/r for every charge, with signs.
All the charges are the same distance from the centre, so V = n kq/R.
The field is a vector and the individual fields cancel at the centre; the potentials do not.

levels.title: Where is it zero?
levels.adds: New idea: with opposite charges the potential is zero at two points on the line, found from the ratio of the charges (Ex 2.1).
hints: Set kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0: the distances are in the ratio of the charge magnitudes.
One zero lies between the charges, one lies outside, on the side of the smaller charge.
Slide the probe: the meter changes sign as you cross a zero.

levels.title: The dipole’s potential
levels.adds: New idea: a dipole’s potential is kp cos θ / r², and it is zero on the whole equatorial plane.
hints: V = k p cos θ / r², with p = q × 2a and θ measured from the axis.
On the equatorial plane θ = 90° and cos θ = 0, so V = 0.
Past 90° (on the negative side) the potential is negative.

misconceptions: Where the field is zero the potential is zero
The potential midway between opposite charges is the only zero
The potential of a dipole falls as 1/r
